per_question.question: What are the general eligibility criteria for CAP/DA services under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
To qualify generally for **CAP/DA services** under NC Medicaid, a beneficiary must meet NC Medicaid’s CAP/DA-specific coverage criteria, including all of the following:

- **Need nursing-facility level of care** under the HCBS standard, as determined by NC Medicaid, and need long-term supports at a level typically provided in an institution, tied to a documented medical diagnosis and functional care need.
- **Show a reasonable indication of needing at least one CAP/DA waiver service within 30 days** of the evaluation, based on the completed CAP assessment.
- **Have a signed service plan** authorizing one or more waiver services to be provided monthly to help prevent institutionalization through coordinated case management.
- If the plan involves **equipment, modification, or technology**, have a signed service plan authorizing that short-term support so the person can return to or remain in a private residence and avoid institutional placement.
- Be **able to maintain health, safety, and well-being** in the primary private residence or another approved setting with formal and informal supports.
- Have **paid care needs that can be maintained within the average institutional cost** of the CAP/DA waiver.
- Have a **primary physician** who can link and coordinate medical services.
- Have an **emergency back-up and disaster plan** identifying who will provide care if key staff or caregivers are unavailable or during a public health emergency.  
  § 3.2.1, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) (effective Sept. 1, 2025; current document per amendment check).

## Consumer-directed CAP/DA
If the person wants **consumer-directed services**, they must meet the general CAP/DA criteria above **and** also:
- understand the rights and responsibilities of directing their own care,
- be willing and emotionally capable of employer-type responsibilities (or choose a capable representative),
- have an approved service plan specifying amount, duration, frequency, and provider NPI,
- receive services in compliance with policy and applicable law, and
- sign and follow beneficiary rights and responsibilities.  
  § 3.2.1, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment).

## When CAP/DA is not covered
CAP/DA is not covered if the beneficiary does **not** meet the eligibility requirements in Section 2.0 or the CAP/DA criteria in Section 3.0. The policy also lists examples of noncoverage, including when the CAP special indicator is missing in NC FAST, the HCBS Service Request Form is incomplete or denied, required assessments are not completed/approved, the person’s needs cannot be safely met through the service plan, or the beneficiary/responsible party refuses to cooperate with the plan of care.  
§ 4.1; § 4.2.1, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment).

If you want, I can also pull together the **Section 2.0 baseline Medicaid eligibility requirements** that CAP/DA applicants must meet in addition to these CAP/DA-specific criteria.

per_question.question: What DME items are specifically NOT covered by NC Medicaid under the Orthotics and Prosthetics policy, and what general criteria must be met for coverage?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under NC Medicaid’s current **Clinical Coverage Policy 5B (Orthotics & Prosthetics)**, the policy specifically does **not** cover certain devices/items, and coverage is allowed only when the general medical-necessity and ordering criteria are met. No amendments were returned for Policy 5B, so the policy document itself appears to be the current authoritative source. [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Items/devices specifically not covered

Policy 5B lists these **specific not-covered categories**:

- **Devices for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience**, or for the convenience of the beneficiary’s caregiver(s)
- **Backup devices** or **duplicate devices** to keep at different locations
- **Devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities**
- **Devices or supplies covered by another agency**
- **Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care** as defined in Subsection 7.3, Coordinating Care  
  [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 4.2.1

## General criteria that must be met for coverage

For orthotics or prosthetics to be covered, Policy 5B requires that they:

- be **ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**;
- be **medically necessary** to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level, and be **appropriate for use in any noninstitutional setting** where normal life activities occur;
- be supported by a **documented face-to-face encounter** with the beneficiary and the ordering physician/PA/NP related to the primary reason for the orthotic or prosthetic, occurring **no more than 6 months before initiation**;
- have the beneficiary’s need **reviewed at least annually** by the ordering physician/PA/NP.  
  [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 3.2.1

The policy also says:

- **Orthotic devices** are medically necessary when required to **correct or prevent skeletal deformities**, **support or align movable body parts**, or **preserve or improve physical function**.
- **Prosthetic devices** are medically necessary as a **replacement for all or part of the function of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part**, and the beneficiary must require the prosthesis for **mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation**.
- Orthotic and prosthetic devices must also be:
  - a **reasonable and medically necessary** part of the treatment plan;
  - **consistent with the diagnosis and medical condition**, especially the beneficiary’s functional limitations and symptoms; and
  - of **high quality**, with **replacement parts available and obtainable**.  
  [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 3.2.1

## Additional general non-coverage rules

Even aside from the item-specific exclusions above, Policy 5B says a service is not covered if:

- the beneficiary does **not meet eligibility requirements** in Section 2.0;
- the beneficiary does **not meet the coverage criteria** in Section 3.0;
- the procedure, product, or service **duplicates another provider’s** procedure, product, or service; or
- the procedure, product, or service is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**.  
  [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 4.1

## Bottom line

NC Medicaid does **not** cover orthotic/prosthetic items that are mainly for comfort/convenience, backups/duplicates, for nursing-facility residents, covered by another agency, or tied to hospice-care equipment/supplies under this policy. Coverage generally requires a proper order, medical necessity, recent face-to-face evaluation, annual review, and consistency with the beneficiary’s diagnosis, function, and treatment plan. [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), §§ 3.2.1, 4.1, 4.2.1

If you want, I can also turn this into a short advocate-friendly checklist for prior authorization or appeal use.

per_question.question: What are the entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria for outpatient behavioral health services in NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:

## Continued service criteria
A beneficiary meets **continued service criteria** if:

### 1) Any **one** of the following is true:
- The desired outcome or level of functioning has **not been restored, improved, or sustained** over the timeframe in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary **continues to be at risk for relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history; or
- The beneficiary’s functional gains are **tenuous**.

### 2) And, in addition, any **one** of the following is true:
- The beneficiary has achieved current treatment plan goals, and **additional goals are indicated** by documented symptoms; or
- The beneficiary is **making satisfactory progress** toward meeting goals and the documentation supports that.  
Cite: [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.2 (effective 2025-04-15; current per amendment check).

A beneficiary meets **discharge criteria** if any of the following applies:
- The beneficiary’s level of functioning has **improved** with respect to the goals in the treatment plan;

- The beneficiary, based on presentation and failure to improve despite treatment-plan modifications, **needs a more appropriate best practice or evidence-based treatment modality** based on North Carolina community practice standards.

per_question.question: How does the EPSDT special provision affect coverage for outpatient therapy services, and what ordering practitioner requirements apply to beneficiaries under 21?
per_question.agent_answer:
For beneficiaries **under age 21**, the **EPSDT special provision can expand coverage for outpatient therapy services beyond ordinary policy limits when the service is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or condition**. But EPSDT does **not** waive requirements that still apply under the policy—most importantly, **if prior approval is required, being under 21 does not eliminate that requirement**. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2025-02-01, current; § 2.2.1; “b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements”]

## Effect of the EPSDT special provision

Clinical Coverage Policy 10A includes an **“EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age.”** The policy ties that provision to **42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r)** and indicates that EPSDT is an exception to policy limitations for beneficiaries under 21, while also making clear that EPSDT does **not** authorize services that are:

- **unsafe**,
- **ineffective**,
- **experimental or investigational**, or
- **not medical in nature / not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment**. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2025-02-01, current; § 2.2.1]

So, in practice, EPSDT may allow coverage of medically necessary outpatient therapy services for a person under 21 even when ordinary policy limits might otherwise restrict them, but only if the service is medically necessary and not excluded for the reasons above.

## Prior approval still applies

Policy 10A expressly says:

- **If the service, product, or procedure requires prior approval, the fact that the beneficiary is under 21 years of age does NOT eliminate the requirement for prior approval.** [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2025-02-01, current; “b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements”]

The policy also includes pediatric visit guidelines for speech-language and audiology therapy that are tied to severity and medical necessity within an authorization period, which reinforces that pediatric coverage is still structured through medical-necessity and authorization rules. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2025-02-01, current; § 5.4]

## Ordering practitioner requirements for beneficiaries under 21

For outpatient specialized therapies under Policy 10A, the permitted **ordering practitioners** are:

- **Medical Doctor (MD)**
- **Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)**
- **Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM)**
- **Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)**
- **Physician Assistant (PA)**
- **Nurse Practitioner (NP)** [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2025-02-01, current; § 3.1.2]

The policy’s treatment-service requirements also state that:

- **A verbal or written order must be obtained before services start**;
- verbal orders must be documented and **countersigned by the physician within 60 calendar days**;
- **verbal orders are valid for up to six months** from the documented receipt date;
- **written orders are valid for up to six months** from the physician’s signature date; and
- **backdating is not allowed**. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2025-02-01, current; Treatment-service requirements section]

## Bottom line

For a Medicaid beneficiary **under 21**, EPSDT can support coverage of medically necessary outpatient therapy services beyond normal policy limits, but it **does not remove prior-approval requirements** and does **not** permit unsafe, ineffective, experimental/investigational, or non-medical services. The order for therapy must come from one of the practitioners listed in **§ 3.1.2**, and services must begin only after a valid verbal or written order is obtained.

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes — NC Medicaid can cover Personal Care Services for a beneficiary living in an assisted living facility, but only if the facility fits the policy’s covered congregate-setting categories and the beneficiary meets the PCS eligibility criteria.

Under NC Medicaid’s congregate-settings PCS policy, coverage applies to a beneficiary who “resides in” a congregate facility licensed in North Carolina as an Adult Care Home or combination home, or in certain licensed group homes, and who also meets the required functional and medical criteria. The same policy requires an independent PCS assessment conducted in the beneficiary’s congregate facility and verification of a valid facility license. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings, § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment); [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings, § 5.4.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

It is **not covered** if the beneficiary does not meet the policy’s Section 3 criteria, and additional non-covered situations include when PCS is provided somewhere other than the beneficiary’s primary congregate living setting, when required assessments are not completed, or when informal caregivers are available and able to meet the need. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings, § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment); [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings, § 4.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Bottom line
If by “assisted living facility” you mean a North Carolina licensed Adult Care Home or combination home, then **yes, PCS may be covered** under Policy 3L-1, subject to the beneficiary meeting the functional, medical, and assessment requirements. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

per_question.question: Can a CAP/DA beneficiary transfer between service providers, and what rules govern transfers of eligible beneficiaries?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. A CAP/DA beneficiary can transfer, and the governing rule is the CAP/DA policy’s transfer section for eligible beneficiaries.

## Rule for transfers

Under **Section 3.3, “Transfers of Eligible Beneficiaries,”** the **CME must coordinate the transfer to prevent gaps in service provisions**. Before the transfer, the following must be completed:

- determine the anticipated start date of service;
- coordinate a transition plan between provider agencies;
- discuss and plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- initiate transfer of the electronic health record in the CAP Business System (e-CAP/DA) to the receiving county;
- arrange a home visit within **5 business days** after the beneficiary moves to the new primary residence, so the receiving entity can assess the environment and identify health and welfare concerns; and
- coordinate services so they begin on the **first date of the transfer**.  
Cite: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 3.3 (effective Sept. 1, 2025; current per amendment check).

## If the beneficiary is transferring to a different county

For a **CAP/DA beneficiary transferring to a different county**, Section 3.3 adds more specific requirements:

- the transferring CME designee must coordinate with the receiving CME designee on the agreed transfer date, or **within less than 30 calendar days of the request to transfer**;
- both agencies must discuss and plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- the electronic health record must be transferred to the receiving county;
- the receiving CME designee must arrange the **home visit within 5 business days** after the move; and
- services must begin on the **first date of transfer into the receiving county**.  
Cite: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 3.3.

## Provider-choice context

The policy also supports beneficiary choice among providers. The CAP/DA person-centered service plan must ensure the beneficiary’s **right to choose among providers** and among Medicaid-enrolled providers, documented by a signed freedom-of-choice form. That supports the general premise that beneficiaries are not locked into one provider, though the actual transfer mechanics are governed by Section 3.3.  
Cite: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 5.4.2.

## Bottom line

A CAP/DA beneficiary **may transfer between service providers / service arrangements**, but the transfer must be coordinated by the **Case Management Entity (CME)** under **Section 3.3** to avoid service gaps and protect the beneficiary’s health and safety. The policy is especially explicit about transfers involving a move to another county.

per_question.question: Is there a maximum earned income limit for people on HCWD (Health Coverage for Workers with Disabilities), and what premiums apply?
per_question.agent_answer:
No—HCWD does **not** have a maximum **earned** income limit in the materials I could verify. The governing change notice says HCWD was revised “to state that HCWD covers individuals regardless of total countable income,” while keeping a **150% FPL cap on unearned income** and using sliding-scale premiums and fees instead. [[CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)]

## Income limit
The current HCWD policy says a person must “meet the income requirements for his coverage group,” and the income section states:

- “Those who have **unearned incomes greater than 150% of FPL are not eligible for HCWD**.”
- It also explains cost-sharing based on **total countable income**. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]

So, based on the surfaced text:

- **No maximum earned-income ceiling was verified**
- But **unearned income over 150% FPL makes the person ineligible** [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf); [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)]

## Premiums and fees
The HCWD policy provides:

- If **total countable income is 150% FPL or less**: **no cost sharing** other than applicable copayments. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]

per_question.question: What is the federal statutory authority for NC's CAP/DA waiver, and what does the state need to demonstrate in its waiver application?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC’s CAP/DA waiver is a **home- and community-based services waiver under section 1915(c) of the Social Security Act**, implemented through the federal HCBS waiver regulations in **42 CFR Part 441, Subpart G**. The federal regulations describe these as “home or community-based services … furnished under a waiver granted under the provisions of part 441, subpart G.” [42 CFR Part 440, § 440.180](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Federal authority

### Governing federal rule
For waiver submission procedure, the state must follow the **public notice process in 42 CFR 431.408** before submitting a new demonstration or extension to CMS. That requires at least a **30-day public notice and comment period**, specified application detail, and at least **two public hearings**. [42 CFR Part 431, § 431.408](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-431)

For the **substantive authority** for an HCBS waiver like CAP/DA, the key federal source is **42 CFR Part 441, Subpart G**:

- **42 CFR 441.301** says a request for this waiver must include the assurances required by § 441.302 and supporting documentation required by § 441.303, and must provide that services are furnished only to beneficiaries who, absent waiver services, would require the Medicaid-covered level of care provided in a hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID. [42 CFR Part 441, § 441.301](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)
- **42 CFR 440.180** defines HCBS waiver services as services not otherwise furnished under the state plan that are furnished under a waiver granted under Part 441, Subpart G. [42 CFR Part 440, § 440.180](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

So, in short: **the federal statutory authority is section 1915(c), with the operative federal regulatory requirements in 42 CFR Part 441, Subpart G.**

## What the state must demonstrate in its waiver application

Under the federal waiver rules, the state must give CMS both **assurances** and **supporting documentation**.

### 1. It must show the waiver serves people who would otherwise need institutional level of care
The waiver request must provide that services are furnished only to beneficiaries whom the state determines would, without HCBS, require the level of care provided in a **hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID**. [42 CFR Part 441, § 441.301(b)(1)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

Related eligibility regulation: the group may receive Medicaid in the community if they would be eligible if institutionalized and, absent waiver services, would otherwise require that institutional level of care. [42 CFR Part 435, § 435.217](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-435)

### 2. It must provide satisfactory state assurances
CMS will not grant the waiver unless the state provides satisfactory assurances, including:

- **Health and welfare safeguards**
- **Provider standards and licensure/certification compliance**
- Assurance that services are delivered in **home- and community-based settings**
- Incident-management protections for critical incidents [42 CFR Part 441, § 441.302](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

### 3. It must support those assurances with documentation
The state must furnish CMS with sufficient information, including:

- safeguards protecting health and welfare;
- records and information supporting financial accountability;
- its evaluation and reevaluation process;
- how beneficiaries will be informed of feasible alternatives and allowed to choose institutional care or HCBS;
- how post-eligibility income/resource rules will be applied where relevant; and
- cost estimates supporting the waiver. [42 CFR Part 441, § 441.303](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

### 4. It must demonstrate cost neutrality
A major showing is that the waiver is **cost neutral**: the estimated annual average per-capita Medicaid expenditures for people served under the waiver must **not exceed** what Medicaid would have spent for them without the waiver. Section 441.303 states this as:

**D + D′ ≤ G + G′**  
meaning waiver and other Medicaid costs for waiver participants cannot exceed the comparable institutional/non-waiver costs absent the waiver. [42 CFR Part 441, § 441.303(f)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

### 5. It must describe the waiver program itself
The application must also describe:

- who will develop the person-centered plan of care,
- the target group or groups to be served,
- the waiver services, each separately defined,
- compliance with evaluation/documentation requirements, and
- whether the state will refuse services when expected waiver costs exceed the cost of equivalent institutional care. [42 CFR Part 441, § 441.301](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

### 6. It must include person-centered planning features
The waiver request must include a **person-centered planning process** and a **person-centered service plan**, including informed choice, conflict-of-interest protections, and attention to the individual’s preferences and community setting. [42 CFR Part 441, § 441.301(c)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

## NC implementation context for CAP/DA

North Carolina’s CAP/DA clinical policy reflects these federal waiver concepts. The policy describes CAP/DA as offering community-based supports and lists state waiver assurances such as participant access, participant-centered service planning, provider capacity, participant safeguards, rights, outcomes, and system performance. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

**Federal statutory authority:** section **1915(c)** of the Social Security Act, implemented through **42 CFR Part 441, Subpart G**, with HCBS waiver services defined in **42 CFR 440.180**.  
**What NC must demonstrate:** at minimum, that CAP/DA serves people who would otherwise need institutional care, protects health and welfare, uses adequate provider and oversight standards, supports informed choice and person-centered planning, and remains **cost neutral** compared with institutional care. Also, before submission, the state must meet the **public notice** requirements in **42 CFR 431.408**.

If you want, I can also give you a **citation-ready attorney version** that specifically ties CAP/DA to **1915(c) waiver elements** in a short paragraph or memo format.

per_question.question: How many days of therapeutic leave from a nursing facility does NC Medicaid allow per year, and what conditions must be met?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid allows **up to 60 days of therapeutic leave per calendar year** for a Medicaid-eligible nursing facility resident, subject to specific conditions. No more than **15 consecutive therapeutic leave days** may be taken **without NC Medicaid approval**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8, effective 2024-08-07]

## Conditions that must be met

Therapeutic leave must meet all of these requirements:

- The resident must be **Medicaid eligible** and **occupying a nursing facility bed for which NC Medicaid is paying reimbursement**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]
- The leave must be **for therapeutic purposes only**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]
- The leave must be **ordered by the resident’s attending physician**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]
- The **necessity for the leave** must be **documented in the resident’s plan of care**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]
- The **therapeutic justification for each instance** of leave must be entered in the **resident’s health record**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]
- The facility must keep a **cumulative record** of therapeutic leave days for each resident, and residents on therapeutic leave must be identified on the **midnight census**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]
- The therapeutic justification is **subject to State review** during on-site medical reviews. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

## Additional limits

- The facility must **reserve the resident’s bed** during therapeutic leave. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]
- The facility is reimbursed at its **full current Medicaid bed rate** for the reserved bed during approved therapeutic leave. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]
- The facility **cannot be reimbursed** for therapeutic leave days that **exceed the legal limit**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]
- Therapeutic leave **does not apply** when the resident is absent **to receive inpatient or nursing services elsewhere, or at a different level of care in the same facility, if Medicaid is paying for those services**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]
- **Ambulance transportation** to the therapeutic leave site is **not reimbursed by Medicaid**, because it is not considered an emergency. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

## Bottom line

**60 days per calendar year**, with:
- **physician order,**
- **therapeutic purpose,**
- **documentation in the care plan and health record,**
- and **NC Medicaid approval if more than 15 consecutive days** are requested.  

I checked amendments for Policy **2B-1** and the current authoritative document remains **[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)**, effective **August 7, 2024**.

per_question.question: If a Private Duty Nursing provider terminates services for a Medicaid beneficiary, what notification requirements must they follow?
per_question.agent_answer:
A PDN provider that terminates or discharges services must notify NC Medicaid within **5 business days**, and the exact submission depends on why services ended.

## Required notice to NC Medicaid

Under **Section 5.2.4.1, “Notification of Termination,”** of the current **[3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)** policy:

- **If the PDN provider discharges the beneficiary:**  
  The provider must submit the **DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form)** to NC Medicaid **within five (5) business days**.

- **If the provider discharges the beneficiary from Medicaid coverage because another source of nursing coverage is available:**  
  The provider must **notify NC Medicaid** and submit the **DMA-3513 within five (5) business days**.  
  The notice must include:
  - the **last date PDN services were provided** and can be billed to Medicaid; and
  - the **name of the other source of coverage**.

- **If the attending physician terminates PDN services:**  
  The PDN provider must send NC Medicaid, **within five (5) business days**:
  - the **attending physician’s order to terminate PDN services**, and
  - the **DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form)**.

## Appeal-related point

The policy also states that **the decision of the beneficiary’s attending physician and/or the PDN provider to discharge the beneficiary cannot be appealed to NC Medicaid.**  
But if **NC Medicaid** terminates PDN because eligibility, policy criteria, or medical necessity is not met, **NC Medicaid or its designee must provide written notice of the adverse decision to the beneficiary/legal representative, including appeal rights.** [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment), § 5.2.4.1.

## Managed care notice standards

If the beneficiary is in managed care and the termination is being made through the plan, federal managed care rules require required notices to be given in a manner that is understandable and accessible, including for critical written materials such as **termination notices**. See **[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)**, § 438.10.

## Bottom line

For a provider-initiated PDN termination, the clearest NC Medicaid requirement I found is:

- **submit the DMA-3513 to NC Medicaid within 5 business days**, and
- if termination is due to other coverage, also include the **last Medicaid billable date** and the **other coverage source**;
- if termination is ordered by the physician, also submit the **physician’s termination order** within **5 business days**.

I checked amendment status for both **3G-1** and **42 CFR Part 438**, and the corpus identifies each as the current authoritative document.

per_question.question: What does federal law define as 'home health services' under Medicaid, and where must they be provided?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal Medicaid law, **“home health services”** are the services listed in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(b)** when they are provided to a beneficiary **at the beneficiary’s place of residence** and under the required practitioner orders and plan-of-care rules. Those services include:

- **Nursing services** on a part-time or intermittent basis;
- **Home health aide services**;
- **Medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** suitable for use in normal life settings; and
- **Physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech pathology/audiology services** as an optional home health service category.  
  [[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70]

## Where they must be provided

Federal law says home health services must be provided **“at [the beneficiary’s] place of residence.”** [[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(a)(1)]

It also states that, for this purpose, a beneficiary’s place of residence **does not include**:

- a **hospital**,
- a **nursing facility**, or
- an **intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID)**,

**except** for certain home health services in an ICF/IID that the facility itself is not required to provide. [[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c)]

The regulation further makes clear that home health services **may be provided in any setting in which normal life activities take place**, other than:

- a hospital,
- a nursing facility,
- an ICF/IID, or
- **any setting where Medicaid payment is or could be made for inpatient services that include room and board**.  
  [[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c)(1)]

Federal law also expressly says home health services **cannot be limited to beneficiaries who are homebound**. [[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c)(1)]

## Core federal conditions

For these services to qualify as Medicaid home health services under § 440.70, they must be furnished:

- on **written orders** by a **physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant** working according to state law, and
- as part of a **written plan of care** that the ordering practitioner reviews **every 60 days** for nursing, home health aide, and therapy services.  
  [[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(a)(2)]

For medical supplies, equipment, and appliances, the rule uses a related but slightly different ordering/review standard in § 440.70(a)(3) and § 440.70(b)(3). [[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70]

## Bottom line

Federal Medicaid law defines **home health services** as the specific nursing, aide, supplies/equipment/appliances, and certain therapy services described in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(b)**, provided under the required practitioner orders and plan of care, and delivered **at the beneficiary’s place of residence**. They can be furnished in **normal community living settings**, but **not in hospitals, nursing facilities, or most ICF/IID settings**, and they **cannot be restricted only to people who are homebound**. [[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70]

per_question.question: How does NC Medicaid define 'terminally ill' for purposes of hospice eligibility, and what certification is required?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid hospice eligibility, a person is **terminally ill** when the certification supports a **life expectancy of six months or less**. The policy’s certification/recertification requirements specifically require a physician narrative that synthesizes the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis, and for the **third and later election periods** the narrative must explain why the face-to-face findings support a **life expectancy of six months or less**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective Mar. 15, 2024), section D “Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness.”

## Required certification

NC Medicaid requires **written certification of terminal illness for each benefit period**. The hospice provider must obtain the written certification **before submitting a claim for payment**. If the written certification cannot be obtained within **two calendar days after a period begins**, an **oral certification** must be obtained within those two days, and the written certification must still be obtained before billing. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) § 5.4.1 (effective Mar. 15, 2024).

### Who must sign it
- **Initial 90-day period:** certification must come from  
  - the **medical director of the hospice** or the **physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group (IDG)**; **and**
  - the individual’s **attending physician**, if the individual has one.  
- **Subsequent periods:** only the **medical director of the hospice** or the **physician member of the hospice IDG** is required.  
[Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) § 5.4.3 (effective Mar. 15, 2024).

### What the certification/recertification must contain
It must include:
- a physician narrative briefly synthesizing the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis;
- the physician’s attestation that he or she composed the narrative after reviewing the clinical information and, where applicable, examining the beneficiary;
- a narrative reflecting the beneficiary’s individual clinical circumstances;
- the election period dates to which it applies; and
- the certifying/recertifying physician’s signature and date.  
For the **third and later election periods**, the narrative must also explain why the face-to-face clinical findings support a **life expectancy of six months or less**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), section D “Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness” (effective Mar. 15, 2024).

### Timing rules
- Initial certifications may be completed no more than **15 calendar days before** the effective date of election.
- Recertifications may be completed no more than **15 calendar days before** the start of the next benefit period.
- Before the **third benefit period recertification** and every recertification after that, a **face-to-face encounter** by a hospice physician or hospice nurse practitioner must occur **no more than 30 calendar days before** the recertification to gather clinical findings supporting continued eligibility.  
[Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) § 5.4.1; section D “Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness” (effective Mar. 15, 2024).

per_question.question: Under what conditions can speech therapy be provided via telehealth under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
Speech therapy may be provided by telehealth under NC Medicaid only for a **select set of speech and language evaluation and treatment interventions**, and only when telehealth is **medically necessary**. NC Medicaid says telehealth may be medically necessary when:

- the beneficiary’s medical condition means **exposure to others should be avoided**, or
- the beneficiary is in a **remote or underserved location** where access to appropriately qualified providers is limited.

NC Medicaid also imposes these specific conditions:

- **Telehealth must be adjunct to in-person care, not a replacement**, unless in-person care is contraindicated or unavailable.
- **Telehealth must be in the beneficiary’s best interest**, not for the therapist’s convenience.
- **Telehealth cannot be used solely to increase therapist productivity.**  
  ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), e. Telehealth, effective Feb. 1, 2025; current authoritative document)

In addition, the ordinary **speech-language therapy medical-necessity criteria still apply**. So telehealth does not create separate entitlement to speech therapy; the service still has to meet the policy’s regular ST requirements and documentation standards for medically necessary speech-language therapy. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.3, effective Feb. 1, 2025; current authoritative document)

## Short answer
NC Medicaid allows speech therapy by telehealth when the telehealth visit is medically necessary, used primarily because of infection-risk avoidance or limited access in a remote/underserved area, kept as a supplement to in-person care when possible, and used for the beneficiary’s benefit rather than therapist convenience or productivity. The therapy also still has to satisfy the usual speech-language therapy coverage criteria under Policy 10A.

per_question.question: What medical loss ratio (MLR) must Medicaid managed care organizations meet under federal law, and how does NC implement this requirement?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal law, Medicaid managed care organizations do **not automatically have to meet a single nationwide minimum MLR**. Instead, federal law requires states to make each MCO/PIHP/PAHP **calculate and report** its MLR, and **if** a state chooses to impose a minimum MLR, that state-set minimum must be **at least 85%**. North Carolina implements this by requiring PHPs to calculate both a **CMS-defined MLR** and a **Department-defined MLR**, and NC sets its aggregate minimum threshold at **88%**. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438); [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

## Federal rule

### 1) What federal law requires
42 C.F.R. § 438.8 says the state must ensure, through its managed care contracts, that each MCO, PIHP, and PAHP **calculates and reports** an MLR. It further says that **if a state elects to mandate a minimum MLR**, that minimum must be **equal to or higher than 85 percent**. So the federal floor for a state-imposed minimum is **85%**, but the regulation itself does not impose 85% as an automatic universal minimum in every state. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

### 2) How the federal MLR is calculated
Under 42 C.F.R. § 438.8, the MLR is the ratio of:

- **Numerator**: incurred claims + expenditures for activities that improve health care quality + fraud prevention activities;  
- **Denominator**: adjusted premium revenue.  
A credibility adjustment may increase the MLR for partially credible plans. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

The regulation also specifies important inclusions/exclusions. For example, incurred claims include direct provider claims, unpaid claims liabilities, certain provider incentives/bonuses tied to measurable clinical or quality standards, and state directed payments under § 438.6(c). It excludes non-claims administrative costs and requires deductions such as overpayment recoveries and prescription drug rebates. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

### 3) Federal oversight when a state sets a minimum MLR
42 C.F.R. § 438.74 requires the state to submit to CMS an annual summary for each managed care plan that includes at least:

- the numerator amount,
- the denominator amount,
- the MLR percentage achieved,
- member months, and
- any remittances owed.

If the state contract requires remittances for failure to meet the state minimum MLR, the state must reimburse CMS for the federal share of the remittance and separately report the methodology for calculating that federal/state split. The section text notes it was amended at **89 Fed. Reg. 41276 (May 10, 2024)**. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## North Carolina implementation

North Carolina’s PHP contract implements the federal framework in a stricter way.

### 1) NC requires two MLR calculations
The contract requires each PHP to calculate and report annual aggregate MLR on two bases:

- a **CMS-defined MLR** under 42 C.F.R. § 438.8; and
- a **Department-defined MLR**.  
[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

### 2) NC’s CMS-defined MLR
For the CMS-defined MLR, NC adopts the federal structure:

- numerator = incurred claims + health care quality improvement expenditures + the lesser of fraud reduction expenditures or fraud reduction recoveries, as defined in 42 C.F.R. § 438.8(e);
- denominator = premium revenue minus federal, state, and local taxes and licensing/regulatory fees, as defined in 42 C.F.R. § 438.8(f).  
[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

### 3) NC’s Department-defined MLR
NC then modifies the federal concept for its own enforcement metric. The Department-defined MLR is calculated similarly, but:

- may include certain **voluntary contributions to health-related resources** if they align with the Department’s Quality Strategy and meet stated conditions;
- may **not** include certain separately reimbursed required additional directed payments or related-party payments that violate payment limitations;
- subtracts from the denominator payments from the Department reimbursing required additional directed payments, with associated taxes and fees.  
[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

The contract also requires exclusion from the numerator of items such as:

- interest or penalty payments for failing prompt-pay rules,
- certain prior-year rebates or substitute contributions,
- non-claims costs,
- PBM fees and spread pricing,
- marketing/branding materials,
- related-party administrative payments and margin,
- administrative costs not allowed as health care quality improvement.  
[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

### 4) NC’s minimum threshold
NC’s contract says: **“The minimum MLR threshold in aggregate across all contracted PHPs shall be exactly eighty-eight percent (88%).”** It also says the PHP-specific threshold is calculated based on the PHP’s capitation revenue mix using a revenue-weighted approach across rate cells. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

### 5) What happens if a PHP falls below the NC minimum
If a PHP’s **Department-defined MLR** is below the minimum threshold, the contract requires the PHP to do one of the following:

- pay a **rebate** to the Department,
- make approved **contributions to health-related resources**, or
- split the obligation between both.  
[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

- **Federal law:** states must require Medicaid managed care plans to **calculate and report** MLR; if a state imposes a minimum, it must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)
- **North Carolina:** imposes a stricter contract requirement by setting an aggregate minimum MLR threshold of **88%** and enforcing it through its PHP contract using both a federal-style **CMS-defined MLR** and a modified **Department-defined MLR**. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

Amendment status checked: for [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), the corpus identifies that document as the authoritative current federal source; § 438.74 itself shows amendment history in the section text. I could not verify amendment history for the NC contract from the available amendment tool results because the corpus tool for amendments is keyed to policy documents and did not provide separate contract amendment data here.

For NC implementation, it correctly identifies the 88% aggregate threshold, the dual CMS-defined and Department-defined MLR calculations, and the remittance/rebate consequences for failing to meet the threshold. per_question.question: What are the specific criteria for NC Medicaid coverage of CAR-T cell therapy?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid covers CAR-T cell therapy when the beneficiary meets the policy’s general medical-necessity standards and the therapy meets the policy’s specific CAR-T requirements. The specific coverage criteria are:

- **The CAR-T therapy must be approved by the U.S. FDA.**
- **It must be administered in accordance with U.S. FDA-approved guidelines**, including:
  - indications and usage,
  - dosage and administration,
  - dosage forms and strengths, and
  - warnings and precautions.
- **It must be administered at a certified or authorized treatment center.**
- **If the therapy is subject to an FDA-required REMS program**, the treatment center must be enrolled in that REMS program, and providers must be trained to manage:
  - **cytokine release syndrome (CRS)**, and
  - **neurologic toxicities**.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), §§ 3.2, 3.2.1 (effective 4/1/2025; current document per amendment check)

In addition, the policy applies NC Medicaid’s **general covered-service criteria**, meaning the service must be:

- individualized, specific, and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis;
- safely furnishable, with no equally effective and more conservative or less costly statewide alternative available; and
- provided in a way not primarily for the convenience of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 3.1 (effective 4/1/2025; current document per amendment check)

### Situations the policy specifically says are not covered
NC Medicaid specifically does **not** cover CAR-T therapy when, among other things:

- the therapy is **not FDA-approved**;
- it is used **outside FDA guidelines** for indications/usage, dosage/administration, or dosage forms/strengths;
- a therapy requiring **REMS** is given at a facility **not enrolled** in that REMS program;
- the beneficiary is receiving **repeat treatment after prior CAR-T therapy**;
- psychosocial history limits the beneficiary’s ability to comply with pre- and post-infusion care; or
- current beneficiary or caretaker noncompliance makes adherence to the medical regimen improbable.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), §§ 4.1, 4.2.1 (effective 4/1/2025; current document per amendment check)

### Prior approval documentation
If you also need the **documentation NC Medicaid requires for prior approval**, the policy calls for items such as:

- a physician-signed letter of medical necessity,
- documentation of past chemotherapy regimens and dates,
- clinical and social history,
- verification the facility is a qualified/authorized treatment center,
- recent HIV and hepatitis serologies,
- diagnostic/procedure results including bone marrow biopsy, and
- a complete psychological/social evaluation addressing compliance, support network, post-treatment plan, and relevant mental health/substance use/legal history.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 5.2.2 (effective 4/1/2025; current document per amendment check)

per_question.question: Until what age should physicians provide fluoride varnish applications for Medicaid beneficiaries, and what oral screening requirements apply?
per_question.agent_answer:
Physicians should provide fluoride varnish **from tooth eruption until the Medicaid beneficiary is 3½ years old**. The required oral screening includes early caries screening and detection of obvious hard- and soft-tissue pathology in the oral cavity **using a dental mirror and directed light**, plus counseling and educational materials on oral hygiene and nutrition for children, prescribing a fluoride supplement if indicated, and documenting the screening and related steps in the health record. This is stated in current **NC Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy 1A-23, Physician Fluoride Varnish Services** (effective **Dec. 4, 2019**), which I verified as the authoritative current document with no listed amendments. [Physician Fluoride Varnish Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

## Oral screening requirements
Under **Section 7.2, Oral Screening Requirements**, the visit must include:

- **Early caries screening** and detection of notable findings, including obvious pathology of hard and soft tissues in the oral cavity, **using a dental mirror and directed light**
- **Counseling and educational materials** on good oral hygiene practices and nutrition for children
- **Prescribing a fluoride supplement, if indicated**, per the American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines
- **Application of fluoride varnish to all erupted primary teeth**, beginning at tooth eruption until age **3½**  
  [Physician Fluoride Varnish Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

## Required documentation
The beneficiary’s health record must document all of the following:

- **An oral evaluation and any notable findings**
- **Preventive oral health and dietary counseling** with the primary caregiver
- **Application of fluoride varnish**
- **Referral to a dentist, if appropriate**  
  [Physician Fluoride Varnish Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

## Example visit schedule in the policy
The policy gives an example of oral screening preventive package visits at:

- **6 months** (if teeth are erupted)

- **12 months**
- **18 months**
- **24 months**

per_question.question: Can an NC Innovations waiver participant request services that exceed their individual base budget, and what happens if they believe their needs cannot be met within the budget?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. An NC Innovations participant may request services that cost more than their individual base budget if they believe their needs cannot be met within that budget. The policy says the SIS results and base budget are only guidelines, not a binding cap, and medically necessary services must be authorized even if they exceed the base budget. If the request is denied, the LME/MCO must tell the person why and explain how to appeal; the person may also file a grievance about the base budget. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)]

## What the policy says

Under **“Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes”** in **Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P**, effective **Nov. 1, 2016**, NC Medicaid states:

- a participant **“may request services that cost in excess of his or her base budget”** if they believe their needs cannot be met within the base budget;
- the **SIS and base budget are guidelines** and **“do not constitute a binding limit”** on what may be requested or authorized; and
- if the **LME/MCO determines the services are medically necessary, they will be authorized, regardless of the base budget**. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)]

## If the participant says the budget is not enough

The same policy says that if a request for authorization is denied:

- the **LME/MCO must notify the individual of the reasons for the decision**; and
- the notice must explain **how to appeal**.  
It also references **how to file a grievance regarding the base budget**. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)]

## Related implementation point

The policy also indicates that NC Innovations services **cannot exceed the amount actually authorized**, so even where needs exceed the base budget, the participant still needs authorization through the waiver process. In an emergency, the care coordinator must ensure needs are met and process timely updates to the level of care and ISP based on changed needs. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)]

## Bottom line

A base budget is **not an absolute ceiling** under NC Innovations. A participant can ask for more, and if the extra services are found **medically necessary**, they can be approved **above the base budget**. If not approved, the participant should receive written reasons and appeal rights, and may also pursue a grievance about the budget.
